summary.text: 木 depicts a whole tree, with trunk, branches and roots understood as parts of one image.

formation.text: This is a pictograph: the graph represents a tree as a whole, without a separate sound component. An older account describes it as 屮 above roots, but a competing analysis treats the apparent resemblance to 屮 as insufficient to establish a separate component.

components.text: The entire graph is pictorial: its form is understood as a tree, including trunk, branches and roots. These are aspects of one image, not independently established components; the individual strokes cannot each be assigned to a particular part.

history.text: Oracle-script- and bronze-script-style forms are consistent with the whole-tree interpretation. The selected illustrations are modern redrawings, not images of specific dated inscriptions, so they do not establish a sequence of graphic changes or identify individual strokes as particular branches or roots.
The received Shuowen account parses the graph as 屮 above roots. A competing paleographic analysis rejects 屮 as an independent component and reads 木 as a complete picture of a tree.

uncertainties.text: The oracle-bone phrase 埶(藝)木 is interpreted as referring to planting trees, but the inscription rubbing was not checked. The selected redrawings do not represent particular dated inscriptions.
The traditional parsing as 屮 plus roots conflicts with the whole-tree analysis; 屮 is therefore not established as an independent component here.

senses.gloss: tree; use in a tree-planting phrase
senses.text: The oracle-bone phrase 埶(藝)木 is interpreted as referring to planting trees, supporting a tree-related use. This example does not show whether that use predates the wood or board use.
木枋 in a bronze inscription is interpreted as a wooden writing board, supporting a wood or timber use. Its exact date and chronology relative to the tree-planting phrase are unresolved.
Current meanings include ‘tree’, ‘wood’ or ‘lumber’, and ‘wooden’. The evidence does not establish a dated sequence connecting these senses.

In a Mawangdui manuscript passage, 木 is reported as a sound-based spelling for 沐. This borrows the graph for another word rather than extending the meaning ‘tree’ or ‘wood’; the first use of this spelling is unresolved.

limitations.text: The tree-planting and wooden-board examples do not establish which sense came first or a development from ‘tree’ to ‘wood’ or ‘timber’. Dictionary citations for other senses, including ‘coffin’, do not establish chronology.
Reported place and polity names may be proper names or graph loans; their relationship to the ordinary word for ‘tree’ is unresolved.
The Mawangdui reading supports a context-specific loan of 木 for 沐, but neither the text’s composition date nor the first use of this spelling is established.

evidence.text: A tree
Pictograph of a tree.
冒也。冒地而生。東方之行。从屮，下象其根。凡木之屬皆从木。

Pictogram (象形) – a tree: branches on top, roots on the bottom (more visible in earlier forms).
See also 本, 未, and 末.
No known cognate exists. It can perhaps be compared with Proto-Karen *məŋᴮ (“trunk (of a tree); firewood”) (Starostin) or Proto-Lolo-Burmese *ʔmuk (“stump (of a tree)”) (Schuessler, 2007).
The common Sino-Tibetan root for “tree; wood” is *siŋ ~ sik, represented by 薪 (OC *siŋ, “firewood”).
冒也。冒地而生。東方之行。从屮，下象其根。凡木之屬皆从木。

evidence.field: 形義通解 / early graphic form
evidence.text: The entry describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a whole tree, with branches above and roots below, and identifies the original sense as ‘tree’. This supports a pictographic account; the graph has no separate phonetic component.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.text: The entry cites the *Shuowen* analysis ‘從屮，下象其根’ but argues that 木 is not actually composed of 屮: it quotes Wang Yun’s objection that the upper shapes merely resemble one another and characterizes 木 as a complete-body pictograph. This directly qualifies the traditional segmentation; it does not propose an alternate sound component.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.text: The entry reports an oracle-bone occurrence in 《合集》5749, 埶(藝)木, interpreted as planting trees. It also reports 木 used as a place name in 《合集》37789 and a polity name in 《合集》33193. The latter uses may be names or graph loans; the entry does not establish a semantic development from ‘tree’ to those names.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.text: The entry cites the Western Zhou-period bronze inscription 散氏盤 for 木 in 桹木道, apparently a tree-name or place-name, and 曶鼎 for 木枋, interpreted as a wooden writing board. It notes a transmitted-text counterpart using 方 ‘board’. The entry does not provide an exact inscription date.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.text: The entry notes that oracle-bone 木 forms can be confused with a shortened form of 燎/尞, a graphic resemblance/confusion issue, not evidence that 木 itself arose through corruption. It separately records 木 used as a loan for 沐 in the Mawangdui silk manuscript 《胎產書》, line 5, and compares 木猴 with 沐猴 in 《法言》. This is evidence of later phonetic borrowing, distinct from the graph’s pictographic development.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 (Academia Sinica)
evidence.text: The 木 evolution record indexes oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo-and-silk, and *Shuowen* seal-script forms, including bronze catalogue reference 集成08477. Its summary calls 木 a pictograph of a tree’s trunk, branches, and roots. The record confirms broad script-stage coverage, but no glyph image was visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢字「木」：字形演變

evidence.text: The received *Shuowen* text says 木 means growth emerging through the earth, associates it with the eastern phase, and analyzes it as 屮 with the bottom depicting roots. This is a historical lexicographic account; the CUHK entry records a later paleographic objection to treating 屮 as an independent component.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.text: The dictionary lists ‘tree’ and ‘timber/wood’ separately and cites received-text attestations including 《論語》朽木不可雕也 for wood, 《孟子》與木石居 for tree/wood, and 《左傳》就木 for coffin. Its citation list supplies textual sources but generally not composition dates; it therefore cannot by itself establish when each sense arose or a full chronology of extensions.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.text: The entry gives Standard Mandarin mù, Cantonese Jyutping muk6, Tang reading *muk, and Middle Chinese categories 明母、屋韻、入聲 with 莫卜切. It does not supply an independent phonetic component for 木, which is analyzed as pictographic.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.field: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese reconstructions
evidence.text: The entry reports Baxter–Sagart system 1.1 (2014) Middle Chinese muwk and Old Chinese *C.mˤok for 木, glossed ‘tree, wood’. A separate Zhengzhang (2003) system gives Old Chinese *moːɡ. These are reconstructions in different systems, not variant readings and not evidence of a sound component.
evidence.title: 木 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry distinguishes Sino-Japanese on-readings from native kun-readings and describes Old Japanese ki₂ ‘tree; wood’ as a native word from Proto-Japonic *kəi, later written with 木 as a borrowed kanji spelling. Thus 木’s Japanese graphic use does not establish Japanese origin for the Chinese graph. The entry also lists on-readings moku and boku; no historical source for their borrowing dates was established in this research.
evidence.title: 木 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry says no known cognate is established, while noting tentative comparisons to Proto-Karen *məŋᴮ ‘tree trunk; firewood’ and Proto-Lolo-Burmese *ʔmuk ‘stump’. It also identifies Sino-Tibetan *siŋ ~ sik, represented by 薪, as a common ‘tree; wood’ root. These are tentative lexical comparisons and do not alter the graph analysis.

evidence.text: The entry notes that oracle-bone 木 forms can be confused with a shortened form of 燎/尞, a graphic resemblance/confusion issue, not evidence that 木 itself arose through corruption. It separately records 木 used as a loan for 沐 in the Mawangdui silk manuscript 《胎產書》, line 5, and compares 木猴 with 沐猴 in 《法言》. This is evidence of later phonetic borrowing, distinct from the graph’s pictographic development.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 (Academia Sinica)
evidence.text: The 木 evolution record indexes oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo-and-silk, and *Shuowen* seal-script forms, including bronze catalogue reference 集成08477. Its summary calls 木 a pictograph of a tree’s trunk, branches, and roots. The record confirms broad script-stage coverage, but no glyph image was visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢字「木」：字形演變

evidence.text: The received *Shuowen* text says 木 means growth emerging through the earth, associates it with the eastern phase, and analyzes it as 屮 with the bottom depicting roots. This is a historical lexicographic account; the CUHK entry records a later paleographic objection to treating 屮 as an independent component.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.text: The dictionary lists ‘tree’ and ‘timber/wood’ separately and cites received-text attestations including 《論語》朽木不可雕也 for wood, 《孟子》與木石居 for tree/wood, and 《左傳》就木 for coffin. Its citation list supplies textual sources but generally not composition dates; it therefore cannot by itself establish when each sense arose or a full chronology of extensions.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.text: The entry gives Standard Mandarin mù, Cantonese Jyutping muk6, Tang reading *muk, and Middle Chinese categories 明母、屋韻、入聲 with 莫卜切. It does not supply an independent phonetic component for 木, which is analyzed as pictographic.
evidence.title: 木 mù — 汉典

evidence.field: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese reconstructions
evidence.text: The entry reports Baxter–Sagart system 1.1 (2014) Middle Chinese muwk and Old Chinese *C.mˤok for 木, glossed ‘tree, wood’. A separate Zhengzhang (2003) system gives Old Chinese *moːɡ. These are reconstructions in different systems, not variant readings and not evidence of a sound component.
evidence.title: 木 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry distinguishes Sino-Japanese on-readings from native kun-readings and describes Old Japanese ki₂ ‘tree; wood’ as a native word from Proto-Japonic *kəi, later written with 木 as a borrowed kanji spelling. Thus 木’s Japanese graphic use does not establish Japanese origin for the Chinese graph. The entry also lists on-readings moku and boku; no historical source for their borrowing dates was established in this research.
evidence.title: 木 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry says no known cognate is established, while noting tentative comparisons to Proto-Karen *məŋᴮ ‘tree trunk; firewood’ and Proto-Lolo-Burmese *ʔmuk ‘stump’. It also identifies Sino-Tibetan *siŋ ~ sik, represented by 薪, as a common ‘tree; wood’ root. These are tentative lexical comparisons and do not alter the graph analysis.
evidence.title: 木 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tree, with upper branches and lower roots, and gives ‘tree’ as the original sense. This is the entry’s paleographic analysis, alongside its report of the traditional account.

evidence.text: The entry reports 木枋 in the bronze inscription 曶鼎 and interprets it as a wooden board for writing, noting a transmitted-text counterpart with 方 ‘board’. This supports treating 木 here as a graph loan for the word 沐, rather than as a semantic extension of ‘tree/wood’. The article’s text does not independently date the manuscript’s composition.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No separate semantic or phonetic component is proposed for 木 under the sourced whole-body pictograph analysis. The *Shuowen* 屮 segmentation is recorded as a traditional account and disputed by the CUHK entry.

The CUHK entry cites oracle-bone catalogue numbers and interprets their words, but the underlying rubbing images were not inspected; the Academia Sinica oracle-bone database’s interactive search was not run.
The sources establish Shang oracle-bone examples and Western Zhou bronze contexts but do not give exact absolute dates for each cited inscription or an earliest possible date for the spoken lexeme.

A chronology from ‘tree’ to ‘wood/timber’, ‘coffin’, ‘wooden’, ‘simple’, ‘numb’, or ‘stupid’ cannot be securely derived from dictionary gloss ordering. Individual semantic bridges and dates remain unresolved.
The place and polity readings reported for 木 may be proper names or graph loans; their relation, if any, to the ordinary word ‘tree’ is not demonstrated by the consulted entry.
CUHK notes possible graphic confusion with a shortened 燎/尞 form, but no source consulted argues that 木 itself originated through corruption.
The entry provides no independently dated first appearance for the 木-for-沐 phonetic loan beyond its Mawangdui manuscript citation.

Japanese on-readings moku/boku and native kun-reading ki have different histories; this research did not establish exact dates for the Sino-Japanese borrowing layers. Japanese ki is analyzed as native Old Japanese and 木 as its borrowed spelling.

Direct opening of the CUHK search.php URL timed out, but the same character material was accessible and inspected at oraclePiece.php. CText returned HTTP 403; the Baxter–Sagart project page returned an internal fetch error.
The proposed Commons candidates are modern vector redrawings rather than photos of ancient artifacts; no pixel-level inspection was performed in this stage.
The bronze-style Commons page credits a source image identifier but does not identify a specific inscription, object, or narrower period for that selected form.
